enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Not assessable (qualitative case study with interviews and fieldwork conducted between 2015 and 2018; no longitudinal cohort panel or participant retention tracking reported).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative institutional analysis under Ostrom's IAD framework rather than quantitative causal effect estimation; biophysical drought conditions, municipal infrastructure obsolescence, and political-economic power asymmetries are examined narratively as exogenous contextual factors on PDF pp. 11-14).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Formal federal and state water governance norms are accurately cited (Decreto 24.643/1934 Código de Águas; Lei 9.433/1997 PNRH/Singreh; Decreto 5.995/2006 SGIB; 2001 CBHSF decree; Portaria MI 603/2012 on Codevasf; PISF EIA and CGU/TCU Program 81 audit) and systematically contrasted with de facto rules-in-use (choice, boundary, aggregation, information, and payoff rules) under Ostrom's IAD framework, though de facto enforcement gaps are asserted qualitatively without transparent documentary or interview coding tables.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell) — Data collection triangulated regulatory/audit documents, conversational/open standardized interviews (2015-2018), and in loco visits in quilombola and Indigenous communities, with NVivo 11 pragmatic language analysis reported (PDF pp. 8-9). However, no interview guide, coding dictionary, or direct verbatim interviewee quotes are presented in the Results section, making it difficult to distinguish primary empirical observations from secondary documentary synthesis.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (qualitative diagnostic only) — Water distribution inequalities, municipal secondary network collapses, degraded strategic reservoirs, vulnerable canal access enforcement across private lands, and loss of ~1,250 km2 of Caatinga in Pipipã territory are described qualitatively from interviews, field visits, and secondary reports (PDF pp. 11-15) without standardized primary outcome indicators, utility performance datasets, or household-level verification.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern — Although the paper reports across all theoretical components of Ostrom's IAD framework (actors, rules-in-use, exogenous variables, interactions, outcomes), it omits basic empirical reporting details (total number of interviews, interview durations, codebook structure, and direct participant quotations) and blends primary interview findings with literature/audit citations without source-level attribution in Results (PDF pp. 9-15).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell) — Purposive stakeholder selection across five governance categories is described (PDF p. 8), covering federal/state agencies (MI, APAC/Prorural, Compesa, Codevasf), researchers/civil society (Fundaj, OGA), one quilombola community (Garanhuns), and two Indigenous communities (Ibimirim, Pesqueira). However, total sample size (N), within-group selection criteria, non-response/refusals, and whether municipal officials or large landowners/firms (named among the five actor categories on p. 8 but absent from the enumerated interviewees) were actually interviewed are unreported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The study clearly states its objective to understand complex water governance in the area of influence of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF) in Pernambuco by applying Elinor Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to examine exogenous factors, action situations, actor interactions, and governance outcomes.

A qualitative approach is appropriate because the research seeks to interpret institutional arrangements, informal rules-in-use, power and information asymmetries, and conflicting meanings/cosmovisions attributed to water governance by state agencies, operators, civil society, quilombola, and Indigenous actors.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Structuring a qualitative institutional case study around Ostrom's IAD framework (action arena, seven types of rules-in-use, biophysical conditions, and community attributes) and combining regulatory/documentary review with multi-actor fieldwork directly addresses the stated diagnostic aims.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 3, 5-9 (Introdução; A Análise e Desenvolvimento Institucional; Metodologia)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Authors specify five stakeholder categories and list institutional roles interviewed between 2016 and 2018 (MI, APAC/Prorural, Fundaj, OGA, Compesa, Codevasf, plus one quilombola community in Garanhuns and two Indigenous communities in Ibimirim and Pesqueira). However, total interviewee count (N), how specific participants were identified/recruited, refusal rates, and why two of the five stated categories (municipal authorities and private enterprises/latifundiários) have no enumerated interviewees on p. 8 are not explained.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined documentary sources (PISF EIA, Lei 9.433/1997, CGU/TCU Program 81 report), recorded/transcribed conversational and open standardized interviews (2015-2018), and in loco visits (PDF pp. 8, 13, 20). Nonetheless, the paper omits the interview guide, number and length of interviews, fieldnote procedures, and saturation rationale, leaving data sufficiency unclear.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-9, 13, 20 (Metodologia; Discussão dos resultados; Disponibilidade dos dados)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: No discussion of researcher reflexivity, positionality, power dynamics during fieldwork with Indigenous (Pipipã) and quilombola communities versus federal/state bureaucrats, or potential researcher bias in framing governance conflicts appears anywhere in the text.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-9, 13-15 (Metodologia; Discussão dos resultados — absent throughout)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The Data Availability statement (PDF p. 20) notes that the study derives from a UFPE doctoral thesis, that participants consented to audio recording, and that transcripts were withheld from public repositories. However, formal Research Ethics Committee (CEP/CONEP) approval, informed consent procedures, and community-level ethical protocols—critical in Brazilian research involving Indigenous and quilombola peoples—are not reported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Authors report deriving deductive categories from Ostrom's IAD framework and analyzing textual/audio/video data via pragmatics of language (Mattos, 2010) in NVivo 11 (PDF p. 9). However, coding steps, inter-researcher validation, triangulation rules, and verbatim interview excerpts are completely absent from the Results and Discussion (PDF pp. 9-15), preventing verification of how raw interview data supported analytical claims.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 8-15 (Metodologia; Resultados da pesquisa; Discussão dos resultados)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly structured around the IAD components—actors in the action arena, rules-in-use, biophysical/community variables, and governance outcomes—identifying federal/state decision-making concentration in SGIB and CNRH/CBHSF, fragile enforcement of canal access across private properties, secondary supply infrastructure obsolescence, and ontological tensions between state management and Indigenous cosmovisions.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 9-16 (Resultados da pesquisa; Discussão dos resultados; Considerações finais)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: Valuable conceptual and policy diagnostic contribution to "legal last-mile" water governance scholarship, demonstrating why large-scale inter-basin transfer infrastructure (PISF) and participatory statutory frameworks (Lei 9.433/1997) underperform in Pernambuco due to municipal secondary network decay, weak monitoring of diffuse canal withdrawals, and exclusion of traditional communities. Its empirical weight is moderated by older fieldwork (2015-2018, pre-full operation) and lack of verbatim interview evidence.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable policy/institutional contribution, tempered by limited empirical transparency
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 12-16 (Discussão dos resultados; Considerações finais)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Gonçalves, Paiva Júnior, and Cerqueira (2026) present a primary qualitative institutional case study of water governance in the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF) in Pernambuco, Brazil, applying Elinor Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to documentary sources, field visits, and interviews conducted between 2015 and 2018. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits clear research aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative institutional methodology and IAD-guided case design (Q2: Yes; Q3: Yes), and a coherent thematic statement of findings on federal/state centralization, fragile access enforcement along canals crossing private properties, obsolete municipal distribution infrastructure, and exclusion of Indigenous and quilombola communities (Q9: Yes). However, moderate methodological concerns arise across five domains (1 No and 4 Can't tell items): researcher reflexivity and positionality are entirely unaddressed despite fieldwork with vulnerable traditional communities (Q6: No); total sample size, selection mechanics, and apparent non-inclusion of stated landowner/municipal actor categories are unclear (Q4: Can't tell); interview guides, durations, and saturation criteria are omitted (Q5: Can't tell); formal ethics committee (CEP/CONEP) approval is unreported beyond a brief note on recording consent (Q7: Can't tell); and although NVivo 11 pragmatic language analysis is cited, zero verbatim interview quotations or coding matrices are provided in the Results to separate primary interview evidence from secondary documents (Q8: Can't tell).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 No and 4 Can't tell items out of Q1-Q9)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative institutional case study (documentary analysis, conversational/open standardized interviews, and in loco field visits analyzed using Ostrom's IAD framework)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract/Resumo (PDF pp. 1-2); Introduction and Theoretical Framework on Water Governance & Ostrom's IAD (PDF pp. 2-8); Methodology/Metodologia (PDF pp. 8-9); Research Results & Discussion/Resultados da Pesquisa e Discussão (PDF pp. 9-15); Final Considerations/Considerações Finais (PDF pp. 15-16); Data Availability/Disponibilidade dos Dados (PDF p. 20).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The Methods section (Metodologia, PDF pp. 8-9) explicitly defines the study as primary qualitative empirical research combining documentary analysis (EIA, legislation, audit reports), conversational/open standardized individual interviews conducted between 2015 and 2018 with public agencies, utilities, civil society, quilombola, and Indigenous communities, and qualitative textual/pragmatic analysis in NVivo 11. Because there is no quantitative empirical component or quasi-experimental comparator, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching instrument per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
